sources.title: Human History Map civilization index
sources.note: Exact Hindu Shahis identity, approximate 900 to 1000 interval, and separately indexed predecessor, neighbor and successor records.

sources.title: Human History Map 700 CE borders
sources.note: Decoded Kingdom of Kapisa, Kashmir, broad Hindu kingdoms and Sind layers used for predecessor geography and point ownership.

sources.title: Human History Map 800 CE borders
sources.note: Decoded snapshot proving the exact target is absent and showing an implausibly broad Abbasid layer over secure Shahi regions.

sources.title: Human History Map 900 CE borders
sources.note: Decoded sole exact Hindu Shahis geometry, coordinate hash, topology, named point tests and simultaneous Samanid ownership.

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 CE borders
sources.note: Decoded disappearance at the atlas seam and replacement by Ghaznavid, Rajput and blank layers while Shahi rulers still survived historically.

sources.title: Human History Map 1100 CE borders
sources.note: Decoded later Ghaznavid, Hindu kingdom and erroneous Karakhanid assignments used only as long-term atlas context.

sources.title: Noémie Verdon, Titles, Cultural History, and Chronology of the Shahi Kings
sources.note: Latest peer-reviewed synthesis of labels, rulers, dates, primary texts, Udabhanda, Kashmir ties, religious plurality and the 1026 or 1027 ending.

sources.title: Kathrin Holz and Ingo Strauch, Approaching Shahi Epigraphy
sources.note: Peer-reviewed survey of Proto-Sharada and Sharada, inscription types, dating problems, the Shahi era, the Dewai inscription and damaged texts.

sources.title: Minoru Inaba, Between the Afghan Highlands and the Indus Valley
sources.note: Peer-reviewed reconstruction of Kabul River, Khyber, Kurram, Tochi and related routes between highlands and Indus crossings.

sources.title: Arturo Annucci, Late Shahi Coinage
sources.note: Peer-reviewed typology, legends, metrology, metal content, circulation and cautious ruler-title chronology for Late Shahi money.

sources.title: Ehsan Shavarebi and Arturo Annucci, Coin Finds of the Shahi Kingdoms
sources.note: Peer-reviewed site-by-site coin evidence for Kabulistan, Uddiyana, Gandhara, possible mints, commercial roles and archaeological limits.

sources.title: Maria Uhlir and colleagues, X-ray Fluorescence Analysis on Early and Late Shahi Coins
sources.note: Scientific XRF study of elemental concentrations, changing silver content, alloy uncertainty and mint reorganization.

sources.title: Gul Rahim Khan, Coins from Hund and the 1996 to 1997 excavations
sources.note: Excavation synthesis for streets, houses, bathrooms, drains, sewerage pots, wells, pottery, ornaments, tools, dice, coins and Kashmir ties.

sources.title: Ijaz Khan, Exploring the Settlement Archaeology of the Hindu Shahi Dynasty
sources.note: University of Leicester doctoral research synthesizing settlements, domestic architecture, artifacts, routes and landscape survey in northwestern Pakistan.

sources.title: Noémie Verdon, Wayhind or modern Hund in Early Medieval Historical Sources
sources.note: University of Vienna sourcebook entry locating Udabhanda or Wayhind on the Indus and comparing al-Biruni, inscriptions and later texts.

sources.title: Luca M. Olivieri, Barikot in Context
sources.note: Excavation context, Hindu Shahi periodization, fertile double-crop landscape, route role and fragmentary Jayapala inscription.

sources.title: Luca M. Olivieri and Michele Minardi, The Shahi Barikot: Vajirasthana
sources.note: Detailed excavation report on the fortified hilltop, temples, reservoir, lamps, dice, game tokens, millstones and mixed medieval deposits.

sources.title: Elisa Iori, Hindu Shahi Settlements and the Fortified Limes
sources.note: Archaeological survey of castle cities, watchtowers, roads, springs, wells, storage pottery, temples and settlement change in Swat.

sources.title: Alice Casalini and Luca M. Olivieri, The Shahi Temple on the East Terrace of the Acropolis
sources.note: Excavated temple phases, stairs, masonry, kanjur, stucco, quarry routes, scale and the limits of reconstruction at Barikot.

sources.title: Anna Filigenzi, Alice Casalini and Elisa Iori, Marble and Stucco Sculptures
sources.note: Excavated sacred sculpture, materials, inscriptions, damaged fragments and cautious identification at Barikot.

sources.title: Ehsan Shavarebi, Shahi Coin Finds from Barikot
sources.note: Catalogue of thirty-one Late Shahi pieces and uncertain post-Shahi types from specific excavated contexts.

sources.title: Luca M. Olivieri, Addenda to the Shahi archaeology of Swat
sources.note: New survey and excavation evidence for residential quarters, springs, a masonry well, stepped tank and Jayapalanagara identification.

sources.title: Adam Hardy, The Salt Range Temples of the Shahi Period
sources.note: Peer-reviewed analysis of Nagara, Post-Gandharan and Iranian-related building traditions, forts, mortar, plaster, domes and vaults.

sources.title: Małgorzata Leńko, Copper Alloy Sculpture in the Shahi Kingdoms
sources.note: Technical study of copper-alloy images, casting variation, surface treatments, workshop questions and the limits of attribution.

sources.title: Natasha Kimmet, Red Clay-based Buddhist Sculpture Production
sources.note: Technical study of Shahi-period clay cores, wooden armatures, molded faces, hand-modeled hair, appliqué ornaments and accidental firing.

sources.title: C. E. Bosworth, Sebüktegin, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Authoritative account of Sebüktegin, the 986 to 987 campaigns through Laghman toward Peshawar and the early Ghaznavid state.

sources.title: C. E. Bosworth, Mahmud b. Sebüktegin, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Authoritative account of Mahmud, attacks on Jayapala and successors, western Punjab conquest and the Shahi line ending in 1026.

sources.title: Xavier de Planhol, Kabul II: Historical Geography, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Authoritative geography of the Kabul basin, seasonal Kapisa connections, passes and long political importance.

sources.title: The Cambridge History of Islam, Muslim India before the Mughals
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis of Jayapala, Anandapala, the 1001 and 1008 battles and the limitations of older battle narratives.

sources.title: Jagannath Agrawal, Observations on the Hund inscription of Jayapala Shahi
sources.note: Peer-reviewed reassessment of the dated Sanskrit stone record, its public works verse and earlier translation problems.

sources.title: University of Würzburg Proto-Sharada Project, Research
sources.note: University research program on scripts, Late Shahis, Buddhist and Hindu texts and the transition to Sharada.

sources.title: Hirananda Shastri, Dewai Stone Inscription of the Shahi King Bhimadeva
sources.note: Primary scholarly edition of the damaged four-line Dewai stone, its Sanskrit, Sharada-family script, restored royal formula and Bhimadeva identification.

sources.title: British Museum, Shahi bull and horseman coin IOLC.5609
sources.note: Museum record for a ten-millimeter, 2.39-gram copper-alloy Samanta Deva imitation found at Begram.

sources.title: Abdur Rehman, The Last Two Dynasties of the Shahis, ANU doctoral thesis
sources.note: Foundational archaeological and historical study of rulers, inscriptions, sites, coins, administration, chronology and source disagreements.

sources.title: Al-Biruni, India, volume I, Columbia University digital edition
sources.note: Primary account completed about 1030, including the Shahi succession, Anandapala and Ugrabhuti, Sanskrit learning and explicit authorial biases.

sources.title: R. C. Majumdar, The Struggle for Empire: The History and Culture of the Indian People, volume 5
sources.note: Scholarly history hosted by India’s Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, used for Bhima, the Kashmir marriage connection and the Vishnu foundation tradition.

sources.title: IGNOU, Castes, Gender and Professions in early medieval India
sources.note: University synthesis of varna, jati, occupations, gender, household hierarchy and the elite bias of normative texts.

sources.title: IGNOU, Organisation of Agricultural and Craft Production in early medieval North India
sources.note: University synthesis of farming, irrigation, craft labor, tools and ecological variation, used only as clearly labeled wider context.

sources.title: IGNOU, Trade, Trading Networks and Urbanisation in North India, 300 to 1300
sources.note: University synthesis of routes, merchants, markets, taxes, money and debate about early medieval urban change.

sources.title: Anatomy in ancient India: a focus on the Susruta Samhita
sources.note: Peer-reviewed medical history of anatomy, surgery, remedies and teacher-pupil training, with debated textual chronology and no local clinic claim.

sources.title: Monica L. Smith, Territories, Corridors, and Networks
sources.note: Archaeological model explaining why premodern polities often worked through nodes and corridors rather than surveyed borders.

sources.title: University of Vienna, Shahi Kingdoms publication information
sources.note: Project methods, corpus scope, peer review, open primary-source platform and explicit geographic and chronological complexity.

proposedOverrides.summary: A mountain-and-river Shahi kingdom whose real centers and 1026 or 1027 ending expose a badly misplaced 900 CE atlas polygon.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact target hindu-shahis is indexed approximately 900 to 1000 CE and was missing both a card and researched override at initial audit.
The separately carded kingdom-of-kapisa record covers 700 to 800 and remains untouched. It is recorded only as a broad predecessor, never as an alias.
The separately carded ghaznavid-emirate remains untouched and is recorded as the political successor after the Shahi ending around 1026 or 1027.
Only world-900 contains the exact target. It is absent at 700, 800, 1000, 1100 and 1200.
The sole target is one Polygon, one ring and 14 positions with SHA-256 5be7f04275d2d1f39b061cb9ececf79104c5691ab986e7badae71f9b3afc9b12.
The polygon includes tested Nandana, Katas, Lahore and Sialkot but excludes Kabul, Peshawar, Hund, Taxila, Barikot, Udegram, Swat and other secure Shahi sites.
At 900 the atlas assigns all tested centers from Kabul through Hund and Swat to samanid-empire, making the exact target geometry a major data mismatch.
The card uses periods for the exact 900 to 1000 map window, covers the circa 822 origins in sections and records historical survival to circa 1027 in its ending.
No appliesTo alias is added. Related Kapisa, Kashmir, Saffarid, Samanid, Ghaznavid, Sindh, Multan, Pratihara and Rajput records remain distinct.
